Horayot 4b:19.english: MISHNA: If the judges of the court issued an erroneous ruling and the entire congregation or a majority thereof performed a transgression on the basis of their ruling, the judges bring a bull as an unwitting communal sin-offering. And if the erroneous ruling involved idol worship, the judges bring a bull and a goat, as it is written in the Torah (see Numbers 15:24); this is the statement of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda says: It is not the court that brings the offering, it is the people. Twelve tribes that sinned bring twelve bulls, i.e., each tribe brings one, and for idol worship they bring twelve bulls and twelve goats, as each tribe is a congregation.

Horayot 5a:1.english: Rabbi Shimon says: They bring thirteen bulls, which are one bull for each and every tribe and one bull for the court; **and for idol worship they bring thirteen bulls and thirteen goats,** which are **a bull and a goat for each and every tribe and a bull and a goat for** the **court.**

Horayot 5a:10.english: Regarding one who had two pieces before him, one forbidden by the prohibition of forbidden fat and one forbidden by the prohibition of notar, and he ate one of them and does not know which one, Rabbi Eliezer says: Whichever way you look at it (what is your soul's desire)? In any way you judge the matter, he is liable to bring a sin-offering. If he ate forbidden fat, he is liable; and if he ate notar, he is liable. Therefore, he must bring an offering. Likewise, in the case in the baraita, since the court issued an erroneous ruling and it is known that the erroneous ruling was with regard to a matter for which it is liable to bring an offering, according to Rabbi Eliezer it should make no difference that the court does not know the precise nature of their error, and they should be liable to bring an offering. Nevertheless, the ruling in the baraita is that they are exempt, counter to what one would expect to be the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer.

Horayot 5a:11.english: Rav Ashi said: Even if you say that the baraita is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer, it is different here, as it is written: “And the sin that they sinned concerning it became known” (Leviticus 4:14), to emphasize from the word “concerning it” that the judges must specifically know what they are bringing an offering for. The Gemara asks: There too, with regard to an individual sin-offering, isn’t it written: “Or if his sin that he sinned concerning it became known to him” (Leviticus 4:23)? From the emphasis in the word “concerning it” one can learn the same lesson. The Gemara answers: In the case of the individual sin-offering, that expression is necessary for it to exclude one who acts unawares. One is liable to bring a sin-offering for an unwitting transgression only if he performs the action with intent.

Horayot 5a:12.english: The Gemara asks: What is the reasoning of Rabbi Yehuda (who obligates even one tribe that sinned to bring an offering)? The Gemara answers that he holds: Four times the term “congregation” is written. How so? For it could have been written “congregation,” but it is written “the congregation.” This is expounded as if the word “congregation” was written twice. And since the word “the congregation” appears twice in the matter (“from the eyes of the congregation,” “and the congregation shall sacrifice”), and in both instances it could have written “congregation” but wrote “the congregation” — behold, there are four.

Horayot 5a:13.english: One of them serves to render each and every congregation liable, as a tribe is also called a congregation; and one of them serves to establish that the ruling is dependent on the court and the action is dependent on the congregation; and one of them serves to teach the concept of drawing, i.e., a tribe that did not sin is drawn after a tribe that sinned and is liable to bring an offering; and one of them serves to teach that a tribe that performed a transgression on the basis of the ruling of its tribal court is liable to bring a bull as an unwitting communal sin-offering.

Horayot 5a:14.english: And what is the reasoning of Rabbi Shimon, who holds that seven tribes that sinned bring seven bulls and the court brings one bull? He holds that three mentions of “congregation” are written. These are: “The congregation,” “congregation,” which he interprets in the manner that Rabbi Yehuda interpreted. He counts the third and last mention of the term: “The congregation,” as in the verse: “From the eyes of the congregation.” This is written in the typical manner of the verse, as people say: “from the eyes of so-and-so,” and the definitive article “the” does not serve to teach another halakha, and therefore

Horayot 5a:15.english: Of those three, one of them serves to render each and every congregation liable, as a tribe is also called congregation, and the other two come so that a verbal analogy can be derived: The term “congregation” is stated below, and “congregation” is stated above. Just as there, above, the reference is to the court, i.e., “the eyes of the congregation,” together with the congregation, for the erroneous ruling is by the court and the action is dependent on them, so too here, below, concerning liability to bring an offering, the reference is to the court together with the congregation, meaning that the court also brings an atonement offering just as the congregation brings.

Horayot 5a:16.english: And what is the reasoning of Rabbi Meir, who holds that the court brings a bull on the basis of its sin and the members of the tribe are exempt? He does not derive a halakha from the difference between the terms “congregation” and “the congregation.” He does not consider the addition of the definite article to be significant. Therefore, he holds that there are two mentions of the term congregation written. The matters are necessary for him to derive: The term “congregation” is stated below, and “congregation” is stated above. Just as there, above, the reference is to the court and not to the public (i.e., “from the eyes of the congregation” — the court’s unwitting error), so too here, below, the reference is to the court and not to the public.

Horayot 5a:17.english: And what is the reasoning of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar? It is written: “Then it shall be, if it was performed unwittingly, hidden from the eyes of the congregation” (Numbers 15:24). From here it implies a minority, as it is written: “from the eyes,” to exclude — not all of them, but some of them worshipped idol worship. And it is written: “For all the people it was performed unwittingly” (Numbers 15:26), to say that even if “for all” is not stated, the intention is for all, at least a majority — yes, but a minority — no. And if so, there is a kind of contradiction here.

Horayot 5a:18.english: How so? They reconcile the two expressions: If six tribes sinned and they constitute a majority of the congregation in terms of their number, or seven tribes sinned, even though they are not a majority of the congregation in terms of population, but they are a majority of the tribes of Israel — they are liable. For even if they are not a majority in every aspect — behold, even the minority is included in the verse.

Horayot 5a:2:1.hebrew: הורו בית דין ועשו שבעה שבטים או רובו - של כל שבט ושבט דשבעה שבטים, וכגון שהיו רובן של ישראל, מביאין פר וכו', דברי רבי מאיר [דסבירא ליה] בית דין מביאין פר ולא ציבור:

Horayot 5a:2:2.hebrew: רבי יהודה אומר ז' שבטים שחטאו מביאין ז' פרים ושאר שבטים שלא חטאו מביאין פר פר על ידיהם - כלומר: פר לכל שבט ושבט. ואמר בגמרא שז' שאמר ר' יהודה לאו דווקא, דהוא הדין לשבט אחד שחטא על הוראת בית דין הגדול, שהשאר שבטים שלא חטאו מביאין על ידיהן פר פר. ואיידי שאמר ר"מ ז', שהוא צריך רובא ממש, אמר ר' יהודה נמי:

Horayot 5a:3.english: If the court of one of the tribes issued a ruling and that tribe performed a transgression on the basis of its ruling, that tribe is liable to bring an offering and the rest of all the tribes are exempt; this is the statement of Rabbi Yehuda. And the Rabbis say: One is liable to bring an offering for an unwitting communal sin only for rulings of the High Court alone, as it is stated: “And if the entire assembly of Israel shall act unwittingly” (Leviticus 4:13), to teach us that there is liability specifically for a ruling of the assembly, i.e., the court, of the entire people, but not for a ruling of **the assembly of that** particular **tribe,** as that is not the assembly of all Israel.

Horayot 5a:4.english: GEMARA: We learned in the mishna the dispute of Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Shimon, and they bring more on this matter. The Sages taught in a baraita: The court knew that they issued an erroneous ruling, and erred in remembering what they ruled, as they do not remember what exactly was the matter about which they issued an erroneous ruling. One might have thought that they would be liable to bring an offering for this. The verse states: “And the sin that they sinned became known” (Leviticus 4:14), and not that the sinners know. For here the sin is not known to the court, but only to the sinners.

Horayot 5a:6.english: The baraita continues: Rabbi Shimon says: Seven tribes that sinned bring seven bulls, and the court brings one bull on the basis of their actions, as the term “congregation” is stated below (further on): “The congregation shall sacrifice” (Leviticus 4:14), and the term “congregation” is stated above (previously): “And the matter is hidden from the eyes of the congregation” (Leviticus 4:13). Just as with regard to the term “congregation” that is stated above the reference is to the court, i.e., “the eyes of the congregation,” together with the congregation, so too, with regard to the term “congregation” that is stated below, with regard to liability to bring an offering the reference is to the court together with the congregation.

Horayot 5a:7.english: Rabbi Meir says: In the case of seven tribes that sinned, the court brings a bull on the basis of their sin and they (the public) are exempt, as the term “congregation” is stated below: “The congregation shall sacrifice” (Leviticus 4:14), and the term “congregation” is stated above: “And the matter is hidden from the eyes of the congregation” (Leviticus 4:13). Just as with regard to the term “congregation” that is stated above the reference is to the court and not to the public, so too, with regard to the term “congregation” that is stated below the reference is to the court and not to the public.

Horayot 5a:8.english: The baraita concludes: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says in the name of Rabbi Meir: If six tribes sinned and they constitute a majority of the congregation in terms of their number, or if seven tribes, which constitute a majority of the tribes, sinned, even though they do not constitute a majority of the congregation in terms of population, but they are a majority of the tribes of Israel — the court brings a bull.

Horayot 5a:9.english: The Gemara proceeds to analyze the baraita. The Master said: “And the sin that they sinned became known,” indicating that liability is only in a case where the sin became known to the court that issued the erroneous ruling and not in a case where it became known only to the sinners. Who is the tanna whose opinion is expressed here? Rav Yehuda said that Rav said, and some say it was Rava who said, that this is not in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer, as we learned in a mishna:

Horayot 5b:1.english: The Gemara asks: And Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Meir, from where do they derive this halakha that the ruling is dependent on the court and the action is dependent on the congregation? Abaye said that the verse states in the passive form: “Then it shall be, if it was performed unwittingly, hidden from the eyes of the congregation” (Numbers 15:24), meaning that the action of the congregation was performed by the ruling of the Sanhedrin. Rava said: It is derived from that which is stated: “For all the people it was performed unwittingly” (Numbers 15:26), meaning that the unwitting error is common to all, to the court through its ruling and to the congregation through its action.

Horayot 5b:2.english: The Gemara notes: And both are necessary. For had the Merciful One written only: “Then it shall be, if it was performed unwittingly, hidden from the eyes of the congregation” (Numbers 15:24), I would say: Even a minority of the congregation sinned, they would also bring this offering. Therefore, it is written: “For all the people it was performed unwittingly.” And had it written only: “For all the people it was performed unwittingly,” I would say: There is no liability unless the court acts together with the majority of the congregation, so that there is one unwitting error for all the people. Therefore, it is stated: “Then it shall be, if it was performed unwittingly, hidden from the eyes of the congregation” — that the unwitting error is performed based on a ruling, and the action of the court is not significant in this regard.

Horayot 5b:3.english: The Gemara challenges: But when these verses are written, they are written with regard to an erroneous ruling involving idol worship, not concerning erroneous rulings involving other transgressions. The Gemara explains: We derive it by means of a verbal analogy between “from the eyes of the congregation” written with regard to other transgressions, and “from the eyes of the congregation” written concerning idol worship.

Rashi on Horayot 4b:19:1.english: If the court issued a ruling and the entire congregation or a majority thereof performed on its basis, they bring a bull - for example, the court brings the offering, and not the public.

Rashi on Horayot 4b:19:2.english: For idol worship, the court brings a bull and a goat; this is the statement of Rabbi Meir - because for idol worship, when there is an erroneous ruling, they bring a bull and a goat. As it is written in the portion of Shelach Lecha: 'And if you err and do not perform all these commandments' (Numbers 15:22), which refers to idol worship, as it states later in the chapter 'Hora Kohen Mashiach': 'Which commandment is equivalent to all the commandments? You must say: This is idol worship.' And it is written (Numbers 15:24): 'And the entire congregation shall offer one bull from the herd as a burnt offering for a pleasing aroma to the Lord, with its meal offering and its libation according to the ordinance, and one he-goat for a sin offering.'

Rashi on Horayot 4b:19:3.english: Rabbi Yehuda says: Twelve tribes bring twelve bulls - because each and every tribe is called a congregation, and he holds that the public brings a bull, not the court.

Rashi on Horayot 5a:10:1.hebrew: מה נפשך - דתנן במסכת כריתות בפ' ספק אכל חלב (כריתות דף יט.) חלב ונותר לפניו ואכל את אחד מהם ואינו יודע איזה מהן אכל רבי אליעזר מחייב חטאת ורבי יהושע פוטר ותניא אמר רבי אליעזר מה נפשך אם חלב אכל חייב אם נותר אכל חייב אמר לו רבי יהושע הרי הוא אומר אשר חטא בה עד שיודע לו במאי חטא הכא נמי סבירא ליה לר' אליעזר מה נפשך אם חלב אכלו בהוראה מביאין פר ואם דם אכלו בהוראה מביאין פר וחייבין ממ"נ:
Rashi on Horayot 5a:10:1.english: Whichever way you look at it - As we learned in Tractate Keritot, in the chapter on one who ate uncertain forbidden fat (Keritot 19b): If forbidden fat and notar were before him, and he ate one of them and does not know which one he ate, Rabbi Eliezer holds him liable for a sin-offering, and Rabbi Yehoshua exempts him. And it was taught in a baraita: Rabbi Eliezer said: Whichever way you look at it, if he ate forbidden fat, he is liable; if he ate notar, he is liable. Rabbi Yehoshua said to him: The verse states: “that he sinned concerning it,” until it is known to him what he sinned concerning. Here too, Rabbi Eliezer holds: Whichever way you look at it, if they ate forbidden fat based on a ruling, they bring a bull; and if they ate blood based on a ruling, they bring a bull, and they are liable in any case.

Rashi on Horayot 5a:11:1.hebrew: אפי' תימא רבי אליעזר ושאני הכא דכתיב ונודעה החטאת אשר חטאו עליה והקריבו. דמשמע שיודע להם החטא שחטאו עליו ע"פ בית דין:
Rashi on Horayot 5a:11:1.english: Even if you say Rabbi Eliezer, it is different here, as it is written: “And the sin became known that they sinned concerning it and offered.” This implies that the sin they sinned concerning must be known to them according to the court.

Rashi on Horayot 5a:11:2.hebrew: התם נמי הא כתיב אשר חטא בה - דמשמע עד שיודע לו במה חטא:
Rashi on Horayot 5a:11:2.english: There too, isn’t it written: “that he sinned concerning it” - which implies until it is known to him what he sinned concerning.

Rashi on Horayot 5a:11:3.hebrew: בה - (פרט למתעסק דבה) משמע דמתכוין לעשות החטא פרט למתעסק בשבת כגון שנתכוין להגביה את התלוש וחתך את המחובר דפטור אבל מתעסק בחלבי' ובעריות חייב שכבר נהנה כדאמר בפ' ד' מיתות (סנהדרין סב:):
Rashi on Horayot 5a:11:3.english: Concerning it - (To exclude one who acts unawares, for “concerning it”) implies that one intended to commit the sin. This excludes one who acts unawares on Shabbat, for example, one who intended to lift something detached and cut something attached, who is exempt. But one who acts unawares concerning forbidden fats and forbidden sexual relations is liable, because he already derived pleasure, as stated in the chapter on four death penalties (Sanhedrin 62b).

Rashi on Horayot 5a:12:1.hebrew: ד' קהל כתיבי - מעיני הקהל והקריבו הקהל דלימא קרא מעיני קהל מאי הקהל תרי וליכתוב קרא והקריבו קהל מאי הקהל תרי והרי ארבעה. חטאת הקהל לא קא חשיב דהא לא כתיב לא בהוראה ולא בהקרבה:
Rashi on Horayot 5a:12:1.english: Four mentions of “congregation” are written - “from the eyes of the congregation” and “and the congregation shall sacrifice.” For the verse could have said “from the eyes of a congregation.” What is “the congregation”? Two. And the verse could have written “and a congregation shall sacrifice.” What is “the congregation”? Two. And behold, there are four. “The sin of the congregation” is not counted, for it is not written regarding a ruling or regarding an offering.

Rashi on Horayot 5a:13:1.hebrew: לחייב על כל קהל וקהל - על כל שבט ושבט דשבט אחד איקרי קהל כדאמר לקמן:
Rashi on Horayot 5a:13:1.english: To render each and every congregation liable - For each and every tribe, as one tribe is called a congregation, as stated below.

Rashi on Horayot 5a:13:2.hebrew: וחד להוראה תלויה בב"ד - כדאמר לעיל (הוריות דף ג.) הקהל ועשו הוראה תלויה בב"ד ומעשה תלוי בקהל וחד למידה דשאר שבטין שלא חטאו נגררין אחר החוטאין ומביאין על ידיהם פר פר:
Rashi on Horayot 5a:13:2.english: And one to establish that the ruling is dependent on the court - As stated above (Horayot 3a): “The congregation and they acted,” the ruling is dependent on the court and the action is dependent on the congregation. And one for the teaching that the rest of the tribes that did not sin are drawn after the sinners and bring a bull for each of them.

Rashi on Horayot 5a:13:3.hebrew: וחד לשבט שעשה בהוראת בית דינו - כדתנן בסיפא דמתניתין הורו ב"ד של אחד מן השבטים כו':
Rashi on Horayot 5a:13:3.english: And one for a tribe that acted on the ruling of its court - As we learned in the latter clause of the mishna: “If the court of one of the tribes ruled, etc.”

Rashi on Horayot 5a:14:1.hebrew: ג' קהל כתיבי - מעיני הקהל לא דרשינן ביה תרתי דהא לשמוש הוא דאתא דאורחיה דקרא דמשתעי הכי כדאמרי אינשי מעיני דפלניא הכא נמי מעיני הקהל משמע מעיני של קהל וחד הוא אבל והקריבו הקהל דרשינן ביה תרי דלכתוב קרא והקריבו קהל מאי הקהל תרי הא תלת:
Rashi on Horayot 5a:14:1.english: Three mentions of “congregation” are written - We do not expound two from “from the eyes of the congregation,” for it came for usage, as it is the way of the verse to speak this way, as people say “from the eyes of so-and-so.” Here too, “from the eyes of the congregation” means the eyes of the congregation, and it is one. But from “and the congregation shall sacrifice,” we expound two, for the verse could have written “and a congregation shall sacrifice.” What is “the congregation”? Two. Behold, there are three.

Rashi on Horayot 5a:15:1.hebrew: חד לחייב על כל קהל וקהל - דר"ש נמי ס"ל דשבט אחד איקרי קהל אייתרי ליה תרי לג"ש נאמר קהל למעלה וכו':
Rashi on Horayot 5a:15:1.english: One to render each and every congregation liable - For Rabbi Shimon also holds that one tribe is called a congregation. Two remain for a verbal analogy: “congregation” is stated above, etc.

Rashi on Horayot 5a:17:1.hebrew: ור"ש בן אלעזר מ"ט - דכתיב בהוראה דעבודת כוכבים בפרשת שלח לך אנשים והיה אם מעיני העדה אלמא אפי' מיעוטא חטאו מביאין פר ושעירה דכתיב מעיני משמע מקצת עיני ולא כל עיני וכתיב כי לכל משמע דרובא אין דרובו ככולו ומיעוטא לא הא כיצד וכו' דמעיני אפי' מיעוט קהל כגון ברוב שבטים והאי דכתי' כי לכל דבעינן רובא דקהל אפילו במיעוט שבטים:
Rashi on Horayot 5a:17:1.english: And what is the reasoning of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar? - For it is written regarding a ruling concerning idol worship in Parashat Shelach Lecha Anashim: “Then it shall be, if it was performed unwittingly, hidden from the eyes of the congregation.” Apparently, even if a minority sinned, they bring a bull and a goat, for “from the eyes” implies some eyes and not all eyes. And it is written: “For all,” which implies that a majority, yes, for a majority is like the entirety, but a minority, no. How so? etc. That “from the eyes” refers even to a minority of the congregation, such as a majority of tribes. And this “for all” implies that we require a majority of the congregation, even if it is a minority of tribes.

Rashi on Horayot 5a:1:1.english: Rabbi Shimon says: Thirteen bulls - one bull for each and every tribe and one bull for the court. And the reasoning for all of them is explained in the Gemara.

Rashi on Horayot 5a:2:1.english: If the court issued a ruling and seven tribes or a majority thereof performed - a majority of each and every one of the seven tribes, and for example, they constituted a majority of Israel, they bring a bull, etc.; these are the words of Rabbi Meir, who holds that the court brings a bull and not the public.

Rashi on Horayot 5a:2:2.english: Rabbi Yehuda says: Seven tribes that sinned bring seven bulls, and the rest of the tribes that did not sin bring one bull each on their behalf - meaning, one bull for each and every tribe. And it is stated in the Gemara that the 'seven' that Rabbi Yehuda mentioned is not precise, for the same applies to one tribe that sinned based on the ruling of the High Court, that the rest of the tribes that did not sin bring one bull each on their behalf. And since Rabbi Meir mentioned 'seven' because he requires an actual majority, Rabbi Yehuda also mentioned 'seven'.

Rashi on Horayot 5a:3:1.english: And the Rabbis say: They are liable to bring a bull only for a ruling of the High Court - but a single tribe acting on the ruling of its own court is considered like an unwitting action, and each person brings a female lamb or a female goat.

Rashi on Horayot 5a:3:2.english: The assembly of Israel - this refers to the Sanhedrin, meaning the Sanhedrin of Israel, which is the High Court.

Rashi on Horayot 5a:4:1.hebrew: ידעו שהורו וטעו מה שהורו - כלומר הורו ב"ד שחלב מותר בבטול מקצת ועשו קהל על פיהן ואכלו שוגגין חלב ודם דהוי חד בשגגת מעשה בלבד וחד בהוראה ואח"כ ידעו שהורו שלא כראוי אלא שטעו במה שהורו דאינם יודעים אם על החלב הורו או על הדם יכול יהו חייבין פר דליהוי הוראה מעליא: החוטאין: דלא סגי בידיעה דחוטאין דאע"ג דעשו בהוראה דממה נפשך חד מנייהו בהורא' הוה דהא אכלי לתרווייהו חלב ודם אפ"ה פטורין דצריך שיברר להם אותו חטא שעשו בהוראה:
Rashi on Horayot 5a:4:1.english: They knew that they ruled and erred in what they ruled - That is to say, the court ruled that forbidden fat is permitted in partial nullification, and the congregation acted according to their ruling and unwittingly ate forbidden fat and blood, where one was only an unwitting act and one was due to a ruling. And afterwards, they knew that they ruled improperly, but they erred in what they ruled, as they do not know if they ruled concerning forbidden fat or concerning blood. One might think they would be liable for a bull, as it would be a proper ruling.

Rashi on Horayot 5a:4:2.hebrew: ת"ל ונודעה החטאת - אשר חטאו עליה והקריבו כלומר דצריך שיודע החטאת שיהיו יודעין על מה הורו אם על החלב או על הדם:
Rashi on Horayot 5a:4:2.english: The verse states: “And the sin became known” - that they sinned concerning it and offered. That is to say, it is necessary that the sin be known, that they know what they ruled concerning, whether concerning forbidden fat or concerning blood.

Rashi on Horayot 5a:4:3.hebrew: ולא שידעו החוטאין - דלא סגי בידיעה דחוטאין דאע"ג דעשו בהוראה דממה נפשך חד מנייהו בהורא' הוה דהא אכלי לתרווייהו חלב ודם אפ"ה פטורין דצריך שיברר להם אותו חטא שעשו בהוראה:
Rashi on Horayot 5a:4:3.english: And not that the sinners know - for the knowledge of the sinners is not sufficient. For even though they acted based on a ruling, and in any case, one of them was based on a ruling, as they ate both forbidden fat and blood, nevertheless, they are exempt, for it is necessary that the court clarify for them the sin they committed based on the ruling.

Rashi on Horayot 5a:5:1.hebrew: חטאו שני שבטים מביאין ב' פרים - והוא הדין דכי חטא שבט אחד שמביא פר אחד והא קמ"ל דשני שבטים לא סגי להו בפר אחד:
Rashi on Horayot 5a:5:1.english: If two tribes sinned, they bring two bulls - And the same applies if one tribe sinned, it brings one bull. This teaches us that two tribes are not satisfied with one bull.

Rashi on Horayot 5a:5:2.hebrew: לחייב על כל קהל וקהל - דשבט אחד איקרי קהל כדמפרש טעמא לקמן:
Rashi on Horayot 5a:5:2.english: To render each and every congregation liable - For one tribe is called a congregation, as the reason is explained below.

Rashi on Horayot 5a:6:1.hebrew: מה הקהל האמור למעלה ב"ד עם הקהל - דתרוייהו כתיב למעלה ב"ד עם קהל דכתיב ונעלם דבר מעיני הקהל דהאי מעיני היינו ב"ד:
Rashi on Horayot 5a:6:1.english: Just as the congregation stated above refers to the court together with the congregation - For both are written above, the court together with the congregation, as it is written: “And the matter is hidden from the eyes of the congregation,” and this “eyes” refers to the court.

Rashi on Horayot 5a:6:2.hebrew: אף קהל האמור למטה - והקריבו הקהל ב"ד עם הקהל:
Rashi on Horayot 5a:6:2.english: So too the congregation stated below - “And the congregation shall sacrifice” refers to the court together with the congregation.

Rashi on Horayot 5a:7:1.hebrew: הכי דריש ר"מ מה קהל האמור למעלה ונעלם דבר מעיני הקהל בית דין ולא קהל כלומר דהוראה תלויה היא בב"ד ולא בקהל דהא לא כתיב ונעלם מקהל אלא מעיני הקהל דמשמע מב"ד של קהל ולא מקהל אף קהל האמור למטה והקריבו הקהל בית דין ולא צבור:
Rashi on Horayot 5a:7:1.english: This is how Rabbi Meir expounds: Just as the congregation stated above in “And the matter is hidden from the eyes of the congregation” refers to the court and not the congregation, meaning that the ruling is dependent on the court and not on the congregation, for it is not written “hidden from the congregation” but rather “from the eyes of the congregation,” which implies from the court of the congregation and not from the congregation itself; so too the congregation stated below in “And the congregation shall sacrifice” refers to the court and not the public.

Rashi on Horayot 5b:1:1.hebrew: ור"ש ור"מ - דדרשי תרי קהל לג"ש ולא אייתר חד להוראה תלויה בבית דין אם כן הוראה תלויה בבית דין מנא להו:
Rashi on Horayot 5b:1:1.english: And Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Meir - For they expound two mentions of “congregation” for a verbal analogy, and no single mention remains for the ruling dependent on the court. If so, from where do they derive that the ruling is dependent on the court?

Rashi on Horayot 5b:1:2.hebrew: מעיני העדה נעשתה לשגגה - שתעשה לשגגה על ידי אחרים דהיינו על ידי הוראת ב"ד דהוראה תלויה בבית דין:
Rashi on Horayot 5b:1:2.english: “From the eyes of the congregation it was performed unwittingly” - That it should be performed unwittingly by others, meaning by the ruling of the court, for the ruling is dependent on the court.

Rashi on Horayot 5b:1:3.hebrew: רבא אמר כי לכל העם בשגגה - שיהו כולם תלויין בשגגת הקהל וב"ד דהוראה תלויה בב"ד ומעשה תלוי בקהל:
Rashi on Horayot 5b:1:3.english: Rava said: “For all the people it was performed unwittingly” - That all of them should be dependent on the unwitting error of the congregation and the court, for the ruling is dependent on the court and the action is dependent on the congregation.

Rashi on Horayot 5b:2:1.hebrew: הוה אמינא אפי' מיעוט - חטאו מביאין פר:
Rashi on Horayot 5b:2:1.english: I would say: Even a minority - sinned, they bring a bull.

Rashi on Horayot 5b:2:2.hebrew: הוה אמינא בית דין בהדי רובא - ולא יהו מביאין פר עד שיעשו בית דין עם הצבור דליבעי לבית דין הוראה ועשיה כתב רחמנא והיה אם מעיני העדה נעשתה לשגגה שתעשה שגגה על ידי אחרים דהוראה בלבד תלויה בבית דין:
Rashi on Horayot 5b:2:2.english: I would say: The court together with the majority - And they would not bring a bull until the court acts with the public, for the court would need both a ruling and an action. The Merciful One wrote: “Then it shall be, if it was performed unwittingly, hidden from the eyes of the congregation,” that the unwitting error should be performed by others, for the ruling alone is dependent on the court.

Rashi on Horayot 5b:3:1.hebrew: ילפינן מעיני מעיני - כתיב הכא מעיני הקהל וכתיב בעבודת כוכבים והיה אם מעיני העדה:
Rashi on Horayot 5b:3:1.english: We derive it by means of a verbal analogy between “from the eyes of” and “from the eyes of” - Here it is written: “from the eyes of the congregation,” and regarding idol worship it is written: “Then it shall be, if from the eyes of the congregation.”

Steinsaltz comment #2 on Horayot 5a:4.english: A court that issued an erroneous ruling and forgot what they ruled, even if the congregation informs them what they ruled — the court is exempt and all who acted according to their ruling are liable. As in the baraita. (Rambam Sefer Korbanot, Hilkhot Shegagot 14:4).

Steinsaltz on Horayot 4b:19.english: **MISHNA:** If the judges of **the court issued a ruling and the entire congregation or a majority thereof performed on its basis** - **they bring a bull** for atonement. **And** if this error **involved idol worship** - **they bring a bull and a goat,** as explained in the Torah (Numbers 15:24); these are **the words of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda says: It is not the court that brings an offering, but the public. If twelve tribes sinned** - **they bring twelve bulls,** as each tribe is a congregation unto itself. **And for idol worship** - **they bring twelve bulls and twelve goats;**

Steinsaltz on Horayot 5a:1.english: **Rabbi Shimon says: They bring thirteen bulls,** which are one bull for each and every tribe and one bull for the court. **And for idol worship** - **thirteen bulls and thirteen goats,** which are **a bull and a goat for each and every tribe,** and another **bull and a goat for the court.**

Steinsaltz on Horayot 5a:10.english: Regarding one who had two pieces before him, one forbidden by the prohibition of forbidden fat and one forbidden by the prohibition of notar, and he ate one of them and does not know which one, Rabbi Eliezer says: Whichever way you look at it (what is your soul's desire)? In any way you judge the matter, he is liable to bring a sin-offering. If he ate forbidden fat, he is liable; if he ate notar, he is liable, and therefore he brings an offering. And even in our case, since the court erred, and it is clear to them that they erred in a matter for which they are liable for an offering, it does not matter if they do not know exactly what matter they ruled on erroneously. And according to Rabbi Eliezer, they are liable for an offering, but in the baraita it is stated that they are exempt.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 5a:11.english: Rav Ashi said: Even if you say that the baraita is in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer, it is different here, as it is written: “And the sin that they sinned concerning it became known” (Leviticus 4:14), to emphasize from the word “concerning it” that they must specifically know what they are bringing an offering for. And they ask: There too, regarding an individual's sin-offering, isn’t it written: “Or if his sin that he sinned concerning it became known to him” (Leviticus 4:23)? From the emphasis in the word “concerning it” one can learn the same lesson. And they answer: That expression is necessary for it to emphasize another matter, that the obligation for an offering applies specifically to one who intended that sinful act, to exclude one who acts unawares, for if he did not intend that sinful act but another act, and in the course of his engagement in something else he caused it and sinned, this is not considered.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 5a:12.english: And they ask: What is the reasoning of Rabbi Yehuda (who obligates even one tribe that sinned to bring an offering)? And they answer: He holds: Four times the term “congregation” is written. How so? For it could have been written “congregation,” but it is written “the congregation.” This is expounded as if the word “congregation” was written twice. And since the word “the congregation” appears twice in the matter (“from the eyes of the congregation,” “and the congregation shall sacrifice”), and in both instances it could have written “congregation” but wrote “the congregation” — behold, there are four.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 5a:13.english: One of them comes to render each and every congregation liable, for even a congregation of a tribe is called a congregation. And one of them (“the congregation and they acted”) comes to say that the ruling is dependent on the court and the action is dependent on the congregation. And one of them comes to teach the concept of drawing, that a tribe that did not sin is drawn after a tribe that sinned, and it too must bring an offering. And one of them comes to address the case of a tribe that acted on the ruling of its court, which is liable to bring a bull.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 5a:14.english: And Rabbi Shimon holds that three mentions of “congregation” are written. These are: “The congregation,” “congregation,” in the manner that Rabbi Yehuda expounds, and another time “the congregation.” And what is stated “from the eyes of the congregation” is the way of the verse, as people say: “from the eyes of so-and-so,” and this is not an additional emphasis specifically to include another congregation, and therefore

Steinsaltz on Horayot 5a:15.english: One of them comes to render each and every congregation liable, and the other two come to derive a verbal analogy from them: The term “congregation” is stated below, and “congregation” is stated above. Just as there, above, the reference is to the court together with the congregation, for the erroneous ruling is by the court and the action is dependent on them, so too here, below, regarding bringing an offering, the reference is to the court together with the congregation, meaning that the court also brings an atonement offering just as the congregation brings.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 5a:16.english: And the reasoning of Rabbi Meir, who does not expound the superfluous terms of “congregation,” “the congregation.” Therefore, two mentions of “congregation” are written. The matters are necessary for him to derive a verbal analogy: The term “congregation” is stated below, and “congregation” is stated above. Just as there, above, the reference is to the court and not the public (“from the eyes of the congregation” — the court’s unwitting error), so too here, regarding bringing the offering, it is only the court and not the public.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 5a:17.english: And what is the reasoning of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar? It is written: “Then it shall be, if it was performed unwittingly, hidden from the eyes of the congregation” (Numbers 15:24). From here it implies a minority, as it is written: “from the eyes,” to exclude — not all of them, but some of them worshipped idol worship. And it is written: “For all the people it was performed unwittingly” (Numbers 15:26), to say that even if “for all” is not stated, the intention is for all, at least a majority — yes, but a minority — no. And if so, there is a kind of contradiction here.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 5a:18.english: How so? They reconcile the two expressions: If six tribes sinned and they constitute a majority of the congregation in terms of their number, or seven tribes sinned, even though they are not a majority of the congregation in terms of population, but they are a majority of the tribes of Israel — they are liable. For even if they are not a majority in every aspect — behold, even the minority is included in the verse.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 5a:2.english: **If the court issued a ruling and seven tribes or a majority thereof performed on its basis** - **they bring a bull. And for idol worship** - **they bring a bull and a goat; these are the words of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda says: Seven tribes that sinned** - **they bring seven bulls,** as each tribe brings an offering. **And the rest of the tribes that did not sin** - they too **bring on their behalf** (because of the sinners) **a bull** for each tribe, **for even these who did not sin bring on behalf of the sinners. Rabbi Shimon says:** When seven tribes sinned - they bring only **eight bulls,** which are seven bulls for the tribes that sinned and another one for the court. **And for idol worship** - **eight bulls and eight goats,** which are **a bull and a goat for each and every tribe,** and another **bull and a goat for the court.**

Steinsaltz on Horayot 5a:3.english: **If the court of one of the tribes issued a ruling,** which was a general court for that tribe, **and that tribe performed on its basis** - **that tribe is liable, and the rest of all the tribes are exempt; these are the words of Rabbi Yehuda. And the Rabbis say: They are liable** to bring a communal unwitting sin-offering **only for rulings of the High Court alone, as it is stated: “And if the entire assembly of Israel shall act unwittingly”** (Leviticus 4:13), to teach us: specifically the court ("assembly") of all Israel, **and not the assembly** (court) of **that** individual **tribe,** for that is not the assembly of all Israel.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 5a:4.english: We learned in the mishna the dispute of Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Shimon, and they bring more on this matter. The Sages taught in a baraita: The court knew that they issued an erroneous ruling, and erred in remembering what they ruled, as they do not remember what exactly was the matter about which they issued an erroneous ruling. One might have thought that they would be liable to bring an offering for this. The verse states: “And the sin that they sinned became known” (Leviticus 4:14), and not that the sinners know. For here the sin is not known to the court, but only to the sinners.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 5a:5.english: It is stated in that verse “that they sinned,” this teaches that if two tribes sinned, they bring two bulls; if three tribes sinned, they bring three bulls. Or does it only say that if two individuals sinned, they bring two bulls; if three individuals sinned, they bring three? The verse states: “The congregation,” to teach us: The congregation is liable, and each and every congregation is liable. How so? If two tribes sinned, they bring two bulls. If seven tribes sinned, they bring seven bulls. And the rest of the tribes that did not sin bring a bull for each tribe on their behalf, as even these that did not sin bring an offering on behalf of the sinners. For this reason “congregation” is stated in this verse to render each and every congregation liable. These are the words of Rabbi Yehuda.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 5a:6.english: However, Rabbi Shimon says: Seven tribes that sinned bring seven bulls, and the court brings a bull on their behalf, as “congregation” is stated below (further on): “The congregation shall sacrifice” (Leviticus 4:14), and “the congregation” is stated above (previously): “And the matter is hidden from the eyes of the congregation” (Leviticus 4:13). This comes to teach us: Just as “congregation” stated above refers to the court (“the eyes of the congregation”) together with the congregation, so too “congregation” stated below regarding bringing the offering refers to the court together with the congregation.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 5a:7.english: Rabbi Meir says: Seven tribes that sinned — the court alone brings a bull on their behalf, and they (the public) are exempt, as “congregation” is stated below and “congregation” is stated above. Just as “congregation” stated above refers to the court and not the public, so too “congregation” stated below refers to the court and not the public.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 5a:8.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says in the name of Rabbi Meir: If six tribes sinned and they constitute a majority of the congregation in terms of their number, or if seven tribes sinned, even though they are not a majority of the congregation in terms of population, but they are a majority of the tribes of Israel — they bring a bull.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 5a:9.english: And they explain this baraita and discuss it. The Master said: “And the sin became known” — and not that the sinners know. Who is the tanna who holds this? Rav Yehuda said that Rav said, and some say it was Rava who said, that this is not in accordance with the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer. As we learned in a mishna:

Steinsaltz on Horayot 5b:1.english: And they ask: Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Meir, from where do they derive this halakha that the ruling is dependent on the court and the action is dependent on the congregation? Abaye said that the verse states in the passive form: "Then it shall be, if it was performed unwittingly, hidden from the eyes of the congregation" (Numbers 15:24), meaning that the action of the congregation was performed by the ruling of the Sanhedrin. Rava said: They learn this from what is stated: "For all the people it was performed unwittingly" (Numbers 15:26), meaning that the unwitting error is common to all, to the court through its ruling and to the congregation through its action.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 5b:2.english: And they note: And both are necessary. For had the Merciful One written only: “Then it shall be, if it was performed unwittingly, hidden from the eyes of the congregation” (Numbers 15:24), I would say: Even a minority of the congregation sinned, they would also bring this offering. Therefore, it is written: “For all the people it was performed unwittingly.” And had it written only: “For all the people it was performed unwittingly,” I would say: There is no liability unless the court acts together with the majority of the congregation, so that there is one unwitting error for all the people. Therefore, it is stated: “Then it shall be, if it was performed unwittingly, hidden from the eyes of the congregation” — that the unwitting error is performed based on a ruling, and the action of the court is not significant in this regard.

Steinsaltz on Horayot 5b:3.english: And they ask: But when these verses are written, they are written with regard to an unwitting error of idol worship, and not with unwitting errors of other rulings! And they answer: We derive it by means of a verbal analogy between “from the eyes of the congregation” (written regarding unwitting errors of other transgressions) and “from the eyes of the congregation” (written regarding unwitting errors of idol worship).

Tosafot on Horayot 5a:10:1.hebrew: אם חלב אכל חייב כו' - תימה מי דמי התם בין בחלב בין בנותר חד קרבן הוא אבל הכא קרבן דעבודת כוכבים אינו שוה לחלב. וצ"ל דה"נ ידעי דלא איירי אלא בעניינים שקרבנם שוה כעין חלב ודם כדפרש"י:
Tosafot on Horayot 5a:10:1.english: If he ate forbidden fat, he is liable, etc. - It is astounding: Is it comparable? There, whether it is forbidden fat or notar, it is one offering. But here, an offering for idol worship is not the same as for forbidden fat. And it must be said that here too, they knew that it only refers to matters where their offerings are the same, like forbidden fat and blood, as Rashi explained.

Tosafot on Horayot 5a:14:1.hebrew: ור"ש תלתא קהלי כתיבי כו' - יש ספרים דגרסי תרי קהל כתיבי וכן נראה ובעי למימר דחד קהל כוליה קרא לאורחא דקרא וחד קהל דרשינן קהל הקהל והיינו תרי קהל. ולר' מאיר חד קהל כוליה לאורחא דקרא ומיניה נמי שמעינן דאיירי בבית דין ולא בצבור וחד קהל לג"ש ולפי הגירסא הכתוב בספרים בעי למימר דתרוייהו אתו לג"ש ולא נהירא. מיהו אפשר דתלמודא בעי למימר לרבי שמעון דקהל האמור למעלה הוא בית דין עם הצבור ואי לא כתיב ההוא קהל ה"א דקהל למטה היינו צבור ולא בית דין ולרבי מאיר משמע איפכא. וע"ק אליבא דרבי שמעון לימא ד' קהל כתיבי ומייתר ליה חד קהל למעשה תלוי בקהל ולא הוה צריך לאהדורי אקרא אחרינא. מיהו ליכא למפרך לר"מ לדרוש ג' קהל כרבי שמעון למדרש מעשה תלוי בקהל כיון דאית ליה ג"ש דקהל בבית דין אמור א"כ לא מצי למילף משם מעשה תלוי בקהל דהא לעיל אמר הקהל ועשו הוראה תלויה בב"ד ומעשה תלוי בקהל א"כ מי שלמד משם סובר דקהל האמור למעלה בצבור מיירי ולר"מ לא ס"ל הכי דבצבור מיירי:
Tosafot on Horayot 5a:14:1.english: And Rabbi Shimon, three mentions of “congregation” are written, etc. - Some books have the reading “two mentions of congregation are written,” and this seems correct. And it means that one “congregation” throughout the verse is for the way of the verse, and one “congregation” we expound as “congregation, the congregation,” and these are two mentions of congregation. And according to Rabbi Meir, one “congregation” throughout the verse is for the way of the verse, and from it we also learn that it refers to the court and not the public, and one “congregation” is for a verbal analogy. And according to the reading written in the books, it means that both come for a verbal analogy, but this is not clear. However, it is possible that the Talmud means to say for Rabbi Shimon that the congregation stated above is the court with the public, and if that “congregation” was not written, then “the congregation” below would refer to the public and not the court. And for Rabbi Meir, it implies the opposite. And it is also difficult according to Rabbi Shimon: Let him say four mentions of congregation are written, and one “congregation” is superfluous for the action dependent on the congregation, and he would not need to refer to another verse. However, it cannot be refuted for Rabbi Meir to expound three mentions of congregation like Rabbi Shimon to expound the action dependent on the congregation, since he has a verbal analogy that “congregation” refers to the court. If so, he cannot learn from there that the action is dependent on the congregation, for it was stated above: “the congregation and they acted,” the ruling is dependent on the court and the action is dependent on the congregation. If so, one who learned from there holds that the congregation stated above refers to the public, and Rabbi Meir does not hold that it refers to the public.

Tosafot on Horayot 5b:2:1.hebrew: ה"א עד דעבדי בית דין בהדי רובא כו' - תימה השתא אע"פ שמיעוט נשארו מצבור לא חיישינן כ"ש דלא ניחוש לבית דין כיון דרובא נינהו בשלמא אי הוי בעינן כולהו ניחא דליבעי בית דין בהדייהו:
Tosafot on Horayot 5b:2:1.english: I would say: Until the court acts together with the majority, etc. - It is astounding: Now, even though a minority remained from the public, we are not concerned, all the more so we should not be concerned about the court, since they are a majority. It would be understandable if we required all of them, then it would be appropriate for the court to be with them.
